Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The failing test `testCoreFunctions` contains assertions testing core rounding functions (round, floor, ceiling) with special floating-point values NaN (Not-a-Number) and infinities. The current issue report points out that these core rounding functions don't handle NaN or infinite values correctly, as shown by assertions like `assertXPathValue(context, "floor('NaN')", new Double(Double.NaN))` and similar for infinite inputs and ceiling/floor functions.

The root cause likely lies in the implementation of these core functions (round, floor, ceiling) themselves in the CoreFunctions class or equivalent in the Apache Commons JXPath source. The test expects these functions to correctly propagate NaN and infinities, i.e., when the input is NaN, the output should be NaN; when input is positive or negative infinity, the output should reflect that infinity correctly.

However, the current implementations probably treat these special values incorrectly, possibly by applying basic rounding math without checking for these special floating point edge cases. This leads to failed assertions when the functions return unexpected values for NaN or infinity inputs.

Unfortunately, the exact code snippet for the CoreFunctions class or its round/floor/ceiling methods could not be retrieved. The test snippet and the report clearly show the problem is in how these numerical functions handle these edge cases, but we can't see any defensive checks or special case handling for NaN or infinite inputs in the obtained snippets.

Thus, the bug occurred because the rounding functions lack proper handling for NaN and infinite values, resulting in incorrect return values that fail the tests expecting these special values to propagate unchanged or with expected behavior.

No recent bug reports appear related to arithmetic or rounding issues, so this is isolated to this numeric edge case handling omission in these core functions.

Next step is to fix the rounding functions in CoreFunctions (or the corresponding class) to correctly check if input is NaN or infinite and return appropriate results accordingly, preserving these special cases per IEEE floating point semantics. This will align the implementation with the test expectations and resolve the test failure.

Hence, the fault is in the CoreFunctions class's implementation of round, floor, and ceiling where NaN and infinity input handling is missing or incorrect.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
